items.prompt: How does a fern spread to new places without ever growing a flower or a seed?

options.label: It sends out runners that root wherever they touch soil
options.feedback: Some ferns can spread by runners locally, but that is not how a fern reaches new, distant ground — spores are what travel.

options.label: It grows berries that animals carry away
options.feedback: A fern grows no fruit and no berries; nothing about its spread involves being eaten and carried.

options.label: It releases spores from clusters on the underside of its fronds
options.feedback: Once those spore clusters dry and split open, the spores are light enough to be lifted and scattered by the slightest air movement.

options.label: Wind carries pollen from one fern to another
options.feedback: A fern makes no pollen at all — that is a structure built only by seed plants.

items.ok_line: No flower needed when spores do the traveling.
items.ko_line: A fern's whole strategy skips flowers, fruit, and pollen entirely.
items.exp_title: Dust that grows into a plant
items.exp_text: On the underside of a mature frond, a fern packs its spores into small clustered cases, and once those cases dry and split open the spores are light enough to be lifted and scattered by the slightest air movement. Each spore that lands somewhere damp and shaded can grow, on its own, into the first stage of an entirely new fern.

items.prompt: Why does a young fern frond emerge from the ground tightly coiled like a spring?

options.label: The coil shields its delicate growing tip as it pushes upward
options.feedback: Uneven growth between the coil's inner and outer surfaces keeps the fragile growing tip tucked safely at the center as the frond pushes up.

options.label: Coiling saves space so more fronds fit close together
options.feedback: Crowding is not the reason for the coil; a fern that grew straight up from the start would take up no more room below ground.

options.label: It stores extra water inside the coil for later
options.feedback: The coil is solid plant tissue, not a hollow store of water; nothing is being reserved inside it.

options.label: The coil confuses animals that might eat it
options.feedback: The shape has nothing to do with hiding from animals — plenty of fiddleheads are eaten by animals that find them easily.

items.ok_line: The most fragile part travels safest curled inward.
items.ko_title: Think about what's inside the coil
items.ko_line: The growing tip is the part that cannot afford to be damaged.
items.exp_text: A fern frond grows fastest on its lower, outer surface while the cells on the inner curve barely lengthen at all, and that mismatch is what keeps the whole frond rolled into a tight coil with its most fragile growing tip tucked safely at the center. As the outer cells keep lengthening day by day, the coil slowly unrolls from the base upward, uncurling the tip only once it has already forced its way past whatever soil or leaf litter stood in its way.

items.prompt: Why can a fern only reproduce where the ground stays damp, unlike a plant that spreads its seeds on the wind?

options.label: Its spores cannot survive without standing water nearby
options.feedback: Fern spores themselves are tough and can survive dry conditions; the water is needed at a later stage, not by the spore.

options.label: Its roots cannot grow without saturated soil
options.feedback: Fern roots grow perfectly well in soil that is only lightly moist; that is not the stage that needs standing water.

options.label: Its fronds cannot photosynthesize in dry air
options.feedback: A fern frond photosynthesizes in ordinary air just as other leaves do; dryness of the air is not the limiting step.

options.label: Its sperm must swim through a film of water to reach an egg
options.feedback: The free-living stage a fern spore grows into produces swimming sperm that can only cross to an egg through a film of water.

items.ko_line: The dependence on water shows up later than you'd expect, not at the level of the spore, root, or frond.
items.exp_title: An old habit that never left
items.exp_text: A fern spore grows first into a tiny, separate plant that produces swimming sperm rather than pollen, and those sperm can only reach a waiting egg by swimming across a continuous film of surface water — a method inherited from algae-like ancestors long before pollen existed. Without rain or dew connecting the two, the sperm are stranded and no new fern ever forms, which keeps ferns tied to damp shaded ground no matter how far their dust-light spores can travel.

items.prompt: What is the small, heart-shaped growth that appears before any recognizable fern frond does?

options.label: A young frond still too small to unroll
options.feedback: An unopened young frond still has the coiled, feathery shape of a fern; the heart-shaped growth looks nothing like it.

options.label: A separate, free-living plant grown from the spore
options.feedback: This tiny prothallus absorbs its own water and food and is where the sperm and egg actually meet, before any frond appears.

options.label: The fern's underground rhizome pushing above ground
options.feedback: A rhizome stays buried and sends up recognizable fronds directly; it never takes this flat, heart-shaped form.

options.label: A patch of moss growing near the fern by chance
options.feedback: It is not a different species growing nearby — it grows directly from the fern's own spore and is part of its life cycle.

items.ok_title: A whole plant of its own
items.ok_line: Small, flat, and easy to overlook — but it is the fern's other half.
items.ko_title: Not a stage of the frond
items.ko_line: This structure is not an early, small version of a fern frond — it is a completely different form.
items.exp_text: A fern spore germinates into a thin, heart-shaped plant only a few cells thick, called a prothallus, which grows independently in the soil, absorbing its own water and making its own food. It is on this separate little plant, not on the coiled frond that comes later, that the sperm and egg actually meet, so every fern alive today began as this overlooked, ground-hugging stage before the familiar frond ever appeared.

items.prompt: How does a fern frond keep unrolling for days without its exposed tip ever taking the full brunt of growth?

options.label: Growth spreads evenly across the whole frond at once
options.feedback: Growth is not spread evenly; a fully open base and a still-coiled tip are growing at very different rates at the same time.

options.label: Older leaflets near the base grow while the tip stays completely still
options.feedback: The tip is not idle — it keeps adding new tissue the whole time the frond is unrolling.

options.label: New tissue is added continuously at the growing point inside the coil
options.feedback: A growing point inside the coil keeps adding fresh leaflets throughout the unrolling, so the frond is still building itself as it opens.

options.label: The whole frond forms first, then simply flattens out
options.feedback: The frond is not fully formed before it opens; new leaflets are still being produced as it unrolls.

items.ok_line: The coil isn't unfolding a finished frond — it's still building one.
items.ko_line: The tip of the coil is where new tissue keeps being added, right up to the end.
items.exp_title: A frond that finishes itself as it opens
items.exp_text: Inside the tight coil of a young frond sits a growing point that keeps dividing and adding fresh leaflets even as the frond unrolls, so the base of the frond can be fully open and mature while its still-curled tip is only just forming. Because the newest, most fragile tissue always stays protected inside the coil until the moment it is ready, the frond effectively finishes building itself at the same time as it stretches out into the light.

items.prompt: How does water travel from a fern's roots all the way up to the tip of its fronds?

options.label: Through internal tubes that run the length of the plant
options.feedback: Water is pulled upward through a network of narrow tubes running from root to frond, the same basic system a tree uses.

options.label: By slowly soaking through the plant cell by cell
options.feedback: Cell-by-cell soaking is far too slow to supply a whole frond; a fern instead moves water through dedicated internal channels.

options.label: Fronds absorb moisture directly from the air around them
options.feedback: A frond's surface does take in some moisture, but the bulk of its water arrives from below, through the plant itself, not the surrounding air.

options.label: Water rises only as high as the roots can push it by growing
options.feedback: Growing roots do not push water upward; the water is drawn up by the plant's internal transport system, not by root growth.

items.ok_line: A fern moves water the same way a tree does.
items.ko_line: A fern, unlike a moss, has an internal system dedicated to moving water quickly.
items.exp_title: The upgrade a moss never had
items.exp_text: A fern contains a network of narrow, reinforced tubes running from its roots up through its stem and into every frond, and water is drawn upward through these tubes as it evaporates from pores in the fronds above, pulling the next bit of water up behind it. This internal plumbing is exactly what a moss lacks, and it is what lets a fern grow fronds taller than any moss cushion could ever support.

items.prompt: How does a fern's spore case fling its spores out into the air?

options.label: It bursts open the instant it touches rain
options.feedback: Rain does not trigger the release; the case actually needs to dry out, not get wet, to spring open.

options.label: A ring of cells around it bends as it dries, then snaps back and flings the spores
options.feedback: As that ring of cells loses water unevenly it bends back under tension, then springs forward and catapults the spores loose.

options.label: Wind physically tears the case apart
options.feedback: Wind carries spores away afterward, but it is not what pries the case open in the first place.

options.label: It is chewed open by insects looking for food
options.feedback: No insect needs to open it; the case is built to open by itself as it dries.

items.ok_line: Drying out is what pulls the trigger.
items.ko_line: Nothing outside the case is opening it — the case does this to itself.
items.exp_title: A trap sprung by drying out
items.exp_text: Around the rim of many fern spore cases runs a band of thick-walled cells called the annulus, and as the case dries, those cells lose water unevenly and bend the whole ring backward, storing tension the way a bent twig does. Once the tension grows too great, the ring snaps forward again in an instant, and that sudden recoil catapults the spores loose into the moving air above the frond.

items.prompt: How does a fern manage to send up fresh fronds after a hard winter has killed every leaf it had?

options.label: Spores that fell nearby germinate and quickly replace it
options.feedback: Regrowing from scattered spores would take far longer and produce a different, brand-new plant, not the same fern reappearing in place.

options.label: The dead fronds themselves revive once it warms up
options.feedback: A frond that has died does not come back to life; whatever regrows comes from a living part of the plant that never died.

options.label: Its roots alone are enough to rebuild the whole plant
options.feedback: Roots take up water and minerals but do not carry the buds needed to produce new fronds; that job belongs to a different part of the plant.

options.label: An underground stem survives and sends up new fronds
options.feedback: Insulated by the soil above it, the rhizome carries buds that were never touched by the cold and can sprout fresh fronds once conditions improve.

items.ok_line: The part that matters was never exposed to the cold.
items.ko_title: The fronds were never the plant's only chance
items.ko_line: Something below ground survived even though everything above it died.
items.exp_title: The part that outlives the frost
items.exp_text: Most of a fern's living tissue is not in its fronds at all but in a creeping underground stem called a rhizome, which carries buds that can sprout new fronds and sits insulated from frost and flame by the soil above it. When cold or fire destroys every visible leaf, the rhizome simply waits, and once conditions turn favorable again it pushes up a fresh set of fronds from buds that were never touched by the damage above.

items.prompt: Why do so few of the countless spores a fern releases ever grow into a new plant?

options.label: Most spores are infertile from the start
options.feedback: Fern spores are not typically infertile; the great majority are perfectly capable of growing if conditions allow.

options.label: Spores can only germinate near the parent fern
options.feedback: Spores are built to travel and are able to germinate far from the parent; nearness to it is not what limits them.

options.label: Most land somewhere too dry or too exposed to survive
options.feedback: Being light enough to travel far gives a spore no control over where it lands, and most land somewhere unsuited to the delicate early stage.

options.label: Animals eat almost all of them before they can land
options.feedback: Spores are far too small and numerous for animal feeding to explain the loss; the real obstacle is where they happen to land.

items.ok_line: Being able to travel doesn't mean landing somewhere livable.
items.ko_line: The spores themselves are fine — the problem is what's waiting for them where they land.
items.exp_title: Built to scatter, not to land safely
items.exp_text: A fern spore is light enough to be carried for long distances on the smallest breath of wind, but that same lightness gives the plant no control over where any single spore ends up. Most fall onto ground that is too sunny, too dry, or already crowded with other plants to let the delicate early stage survive, so only the rare spore that happens to land on damp, shaded, open soil ever grows into anything at all.

items.prompt: What are the small brown dots often seen dusted across the underside of a fern frond?

options.label: Clusters of spore cases
options.feedback: Each dot is a tightly packed group of spore-producing cases, sometimes covered by a flap until the cases beneath are ready to open.

options.label: A fungus infecting the frond
options.feedback: These marks are not a sign of disease; they are a normal, healthy part of the fern's own reproduction, present on every mature frond of its kind.

options.label: Dried sap leaking from the leaflet veins
options.feedback: No sap collects on the underside like this; the dots are organized clusters, not random leaked droplets.

options.label: Eggs laid by insects that feed on ferns
options.feedback: The dots are produced by the fern itself, arranged in a pattern typical to its species, not laid there by any insect.

items.ok_line: Every dot is a small factory of spores.
items.ko_line: Those dots are something the fern makes on purpose, not something happening to it.
items.exp_title: A pattern that belongs to the plant
items.exp_text: Each small brown dot on the underside of a frond is a cluster of many tiny spore cases packed tightly together, sometimes covered by a thin flap that lifts away once the cases beneath are ready to open. The size, shape, and arrangement of these clusters differ from one kind of fern to another, which is often the surest way to tell two similar-looking ferns apart.
